title: That we are to avoid pleasures, even at the expense of life
paragraphs: I had long ago noticed that most of the ancients agreed on this: it is high time to die when there is more bad than good in living, and that to preserve life only for our own torment and discomfort runs against the very rules of nature, as these old maxims teach us.
["Either a tranquil life, or a happy death. It is good to die when life has become a burden. Better to die than to live in misery." — Stobaeus, Serm. xx.]

But to push contempt of death so far as to use it for clearing our minds of honours, riches, dignities, and the other gifts we call goods of fortune — as if reason alone were not enough to persuade us to give them up without this added injunction — I had never seen it commanded or practised until I came across this passage of Seneca. He was advising Lucilius, a man of great power and authority close to the emperor, to give up his lavish and pleasure-seeking way of life and retire to some quiet, solitary, philosophical existence. When Lucilius raised difficulties, Seneca said: "My opinion is that either you leave that life of yours, or life itself. I would advise the gentler way: untie, rather than break, the knot you have rashly tied. But if it cannot be untied otherwise, then break it cleanly. No man is so cowardly that he would not rather fall once than be always falling." I would have expected such counsel from Stoic severity, but it is stranger coming, as it does, from Epicurus, who writes the same thing on a similar occasion to Idomeneus. And I think I have noticed something like it — though with Christian moderation — among our own people.

St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, that famous enemy of the Arian heresy, was in Syria when word reached him that Abra, his only daughter, whom he had left at home under her mother's care, was being sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country — a virtuous, well-brought-up girl, beautiful, rich, and in the flower of her youth. He wrote back to her (as the record shows) that she should remove her affection from all the pleasures and advantages being offered, since on his travels he had found a far greater and worthier match for her: a husband of much greater power and magnificence, who would clothe her in robes and jewels of inestimable value. His aim was to wean her from the appetite for worldly delights and to join her wholly to God. And since the nearest and surest route to that, as he saw it, was his daughter's death, he never stopped praying and pleading with the Almighty to please call her out of this world and take her to himself. And it came to pass: soon after his return she died, at which he showed a singular joy. This seems to outdo the others, since he turns to this method from the start where they only resort to it secondarily, and it was on his own only daughter. But I will not leave out the rest of the story, even though it suits my purpose. St. Hilary's wife, learning from him how their daughter's death had been brought about by his deliberate prayer, and how much happier she was to be removed from this world than to have remained in it, conceived so vivid a sense of eternal and heavenly bliss that she begged her husband with utmost insistence to do the same for her. And God, at their joint request, soon called her too — a death embraced with singular and mutual contentment.
